description: EWoK-style physical-dynamics micro-curriculum with tight local evidence for five contrast pairs without copying benchmark item wording.
notes: Generate 500 documents: 50 each for fall, rise, sink, float, speed_up, slow_down, roll, slide, grow, and shrink.
This is a diagnostic bridge corpus, not the broad physical-dynamics curriculum.
Each pair has several anchor families so the model sees nearby evidence language, lexical variants, mechanisms, and outcomes.
Objects recur across opposite outcomes so cause and evidence, not object identity, carry the concept.

physical_dynamics_profile.definition: Can a model connect evidence about directional physical change, motion, and state/process change over time to the right event/process concept?
physical_dynamics_profile.centrality_rule: The target process and its local evidence cue must appear close together; pair-specific evidence, not object identity or benchmark-like phrasing, should carry the meaning.
generation_guidance: Write compact natural prose, not a quiz, glossary, or benchmark item.
Put the assigned lexical_target and at least one same_sentence_evidence_terms phrase in the same sentence.
Use the configured anchor evidence as concrete event evidence, not as a meta explanation.
Do not use negated opposite-event wording for positive-only examples.
Reuse object sets across opposite outcomes, but let the cause and local evidence disambiguate the process.
For speed examples, include both synonym bridges and physical rate evidence such as faster/slower, more/less distance per equal time, tick spacing, force, and endpoint tendency.
For speed endpoint-risk examples, keep crash/crashed/about-to-crash language on the speed-up side and stop/stopped/came-to-a-stop language on the slow-down side.
For fall/rise examples, include sky/ground and ceiling/floor landmark evidence such as closer to the sky, closer to the ground, toward the sky, and toward the ground.
For direct fall/rise motion examples, use natural local wording such as fell downward, dropped lower, rose higher, or climbed upward; avoid benchmark-like minimal-pair sentence shapes.
For sky/ground fall/rise bridge examples, keep the first-order correlation clean: fall examples mention ground but not sky, and rise examples mention sky but not ground.
Avoid contrast bans that are also legitimate starting-position evidence; ban opposite movement or outcome evidence instead.

For roll/slide orientation examples, avoid benchmark objects and artificial painted-mark wording. Use everyday objects such as shakers, jars, books, trays, and lunchboxes with natural cues about turning over or keeping the same side facing up.
For slide examples, include slippery, wet, icy, slick, or banana-peel surfaces. When lexical_target is slip, slips, or slipped, put it in the same sentence as slide, slid, or sliding evidence.
For grow/shrink examples, use size marks, diameter, outline, swelling, expansion, contraction, drying, inflating, or deflating evidence.

path_shape_policy.guidance: Use path_shape only when it is natural local evidence.

document_types.description: A compact active observation with target process and evidence nearby.
A short play-by-play event where cause, process, and outcome are visible.
A short note that uses a visible measurement cue.
A practical note about arranging or checking one observed event.

discourse_styles.description: A short observation with a visible target process and local evidence.
guidance: Use one or two short active sentences.
Keep the target process and evidence cue close together.
Avoid contrast language and avoid benchmark-like wording.

discourse_styles.description: A compact play-by-play description of one physical event.
guidance: Write like someone is watching the change happen.
Mention the cause before or near the process.
Keep the local evidence in the same sentence as the target process.
Use marks, gaps, levels, surfaces, outlines, or other visible measurements.
Do not write a formal definition.
Keep the assigned lexical target natural.

discourse_styles.description: A practical note about arranging or checking one observed event.
guidance: Write from the perspective of someone handling the setup.
Focus on the condition that produced the observed process.
Do not discuss the hidden contrast.
